segments.narration: For five days Londoners could not see their own feet. In the Isle of Dogs that was literal, in the middle of the day.
It began on Friday the fifth of December, 1952, and it did not lift until the following Tuesday.
An anticyclone had parked a lid of warm air over the city, pinning the cold, filthy air underneath it.
And the city was burning nutty slack: cheap, sulphurous coal, in every grate. The smoke had nowhere at all to go.
Four thousand deaths were counted at the time. Later work puts it near twelve thousand. Britain passed the Clean Air Act four years later.
